column8: Welcome to Battles of History. This is not a battle. It is the background to the battles that follow. In 1980, Yugoslavia was a federation of six republics, with many communities and languages. By the summer of 1991, two of its republics had declared independence. We will show you, slide by slide, how the federation came apart: what was decided, what was said, and what is still argued about. Some chapters describe deaths. We tell them plainly and without detail.

Yugoslavia, 1980 to 1991. On the fourth of May 1980, yo-sip Broz tee-toh died. He had led Yugoslavia since 1945. Eleven years later, on the twenty-fifth of June 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. This page tells what happened in between. The wars that followed are told on the next pages.

Where it is. Yugoslavia lay in south-eastern Europe, on the Adriatic Sea, between Italy and Austria to the north-west and Greece to the south. It belonged to neither the Western alliance nor the Soviet bloc. It had broken with Stalin in 1948, and in 1961 helped found the Non-Aligned Movement.

Six republics, two provinces. Yugoslavia was a federation of six republics: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia. Inside Serbia were two autonomous provinces: voy-vo-dee-na in the north, and ko-so-vo in the south. One party ruled: the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

How this page tells it. Each line is tagged with where it comes from. Some things are in laws and election results. Some are only what one side said. Some were found by a court. We tell you which. Many of these events are remembered very differently by Serbs, Croats, slo-veens, Albanians and others. Where they are, we give each account, and say whose it is.

Many nations. The census of 1981 counted more than twenty-two million people. The largest nations were the Serbs and the Croats. Many others lived alongside them, and some people simply called themselves Yugoslavs. The census used "Muslims" as a category of national identity. bos-nee-ak is the name commonly used today for the community historically associated with that category. The constitution of 1974 gave the republics, and the two provinces, wide powers, and each its own seat on the federal presidency. There was a federal army, the Yugoslav People's Army. Each republic also had its own reserve force, the Territorial Defence.

After tee-toh, tee-toh. tee-toh died in lyoo-blyah-na on the fourth of May 1980. His funeral in Belgrade was attended by many of the world's leaders. After tee-toh died, Yugoslavia's collective presidency became the head of state. It included a representative from every republic and province, and its chair changed every year. "After tee-toh, tee-toh" was the slogan.

Debt. By 1982, Yugoslavia owed foreign lenders more than twenty billion dollars. Austerity followed: shortages, rationed fuel, falling wages, and more people out of work, most of all in the poorer south. Slovenia and Croatia were the richest republics. ko-so-vo was the poorest region. Arguments about who should pay for whom grew sharper.

ko-so-vo, 1981. In March 1981, students at the University of prish-tee-na began to protest. The protests spread. Many demonstrators demanded that ko-so-vo become a republic of its own. A state of emergency was declared. According to official reports cited by the International Commission of Jurists, eight demonstrators and one police officer were killed. Other estimates circulated. ko-so-vo Albanian activists saw the response as repression.

The Memorandum. In the 1980s, ko-so-vo's Albanian majority grew. Many Serbs and Montenegrins left. Serb petitions complained of pressure. Albanians complained of arrests and trials. Why people left varied by place and time, and is still argued about. In September 1986, the Belgrade newspaper veh-cher-nyeh no-vo-stee published excerpts from a leaked draft by members of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts. It argued that Serbs were discriminated against in Yugoslavia, especially in ko-so-vo and Croatia. Serbia's communist leaders at first condemned it. Whether it shaped what came later is a matter of interpretation.

ko-so-vo Polje. On the twenty-fourth of April 1987, at ko-so-vo Polje, Slobodan mee-loh-sheh-vich, the head of Serbia's communist party, met local Serbs who said police had beaten them. He told them: "No one is allowed to beat you." The words were broadcast, and made him famous across Serbia. That September, at a meeting of Serbia's party leaders, mee-loh-sheh-vich's side defeated the group around Serbia's president, Ivan stam-bo-lich, who had been his mentor. stam-bo-lich was removed in December.

The rallies. In 1988 and 1989, huge rallies brought down the leaders of voy-vo-dee-na, and then of Montenegro. Leaders loyal to mee-loh-sheh-vich replaced them. How spontaneous the rallies were is disputed. In February 1989, Albanian miners at trep-cha went on hunger strike against the removal of ko-so-vo's leaders. In March, the assemblies voted for changes to Serbia's constitution that greatly reduced the provinces' self-government. Unrest followed. The official toll was twenty-five dead, including two police officers. Other estimates circulated. ko-so-vo Albanian activists said the vote had been forced. Federal authorities later said their response had answered violence against the police. On the eighth of May 1989, Serbia's assembly elected mee-loh-sheh-vich to chair Serbia's collective presidency.

gah-zee-meh-stahn. On the twenty-eighth of June 1989, six hundred years after the Battle of ko-so-vo, a very large crowd gathered at the gah-zee-meh-stahn monument. mee-loh-sheh-vich said: "Six centuries later, today, we are again fighting battles and facing battles. They are not armed, although even such battles are not yet ruled out." The same speech also spoke of economic, political and cultural prosperity. mee-loh-sheh-vich presented the changes as restoring unity to Serbia. Under the federal constitution, the provinces had exercised broad autonomy.

Slovenia. In 1988, arrests in a case involving a military document sparked protests and the formation of a defence committee. In July, a military court in lyoo-blyah-na tried the journalist Janez yahn-sha and three others. The trial was held in Serbo-Croatian, not in Slovene. In September 1989, Slovenia's assembly declared its right to self-determination. Slovenia banned a rally that the bo-zhoor association of ko-so-vo Serbs had planned in lyoo-blyah-na for the first of December. A boycott of Slovenian goods followed in Serbia.

A new dinar. By 1989, prices were rising so fast that money lost its value from week to week. The OECD put the rise in prices during that year at about two thousand seven hundred per cent. In March 1989, Ante mar-ko-vich became the federal prime minister. On the first of January 1990, mar-ko-vich's government introduced a new dinar, worth ten thousand old ones, and pegged it to the German mark. The World Bank reported that monthly inflation fell close to zero between April and June. But his reforms lost support during 1990.

The last congress. In January 1990, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia met in Belgrade. The Slovenian delegation walked out. The Croatian delegation refused to continue without the slo-veens. A reduced session met again in May, but the party that had ruled Yugoslavia since 1945 never recovered.

The elections of 1990. In 1990, each republic held its own elections, the first with many parties since the Second World War. There were no federal elections. Not all of them were equally free. In April and May, Slovenia and Croatia voted. In Slovenia, the deh-mos coalition won, and Milan koo-chahn was elected president. In Croatia, Franjo tooj-mahn's Croatian Democratic Union won a clear majority, and the parliament elected him president. In November and December, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro voted. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, three national parties won most seats. In Serbia, mee-loh-sheh-vich was elected president with about sixty-five per cent. In May 1990, Slovenia's Territorial Defence command ordered weapons moved to federal army depots. Some Slovenian units kept their weapons, and Slovenian authorities secretly organised a defence network. In July, Albanian members of ko-so-vo's assembly, shut out of the building, declared ko-so-vo a republic within Yugoslavia. No federal authority recognised it. Days later, Serbia dissolved ko-so-vo's assembly.

k-neen. About one in eight people in Croatia were Serbs, the majority in some areas, among them the region around k-neen. In July 1990, a Serb assembly at serb declared the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbs in Croatia. On the seventeenth of August 1990, roads around k-neen were blocked with logs. The barricades became a symbol of the unrest known as the Log Revolution. From the nineteenth of August, Croatian Serb leaders held a vote on Serb sovereignty and autonomy. The organisers reported overwhelming support. In December, they proclaimed a Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina. Croatia's new constitution, in force from the twenty-second of December 1990, described Croatia as the national state of the Croatian nation, and the state of members of other nations and minorities, naming the Serbs first among them. Its fourteenth article guaranteed equality. Croatia's government said Serbs kept full civic rights. Krajina Serb leaders argued that the constitution stripped Serbs of their former status as a constituent people of the republic.

The army and the presidency. In January 1991, the federal presidency ordered illegal armed groups to disarm. Belgrade television showed an army film about Croatian arms imports, with Croatia's defence minister, Martin shpeh-gel. How the film was edited is disputed. On the ninth of March 1991, a large opposition protest filled central Belgrade. Armoured vehicles were sent into the streets. A police officer, neh-del-ko ko-so-vich, and a demonstrator, bra-nee-vo-yeh mee-lee-no-vich, were killed. Days later, the army's leaders asked the federal presidency for emergency measures. The proposal failed to win a majority. The army's leaders said such measures would prevent violence between nations and protect the federation. In the trial of Milan mar-tich, Croatian witnesses described the army as increasingly protecting areas held by Serb forces. On the sixteenth of March, mee-loh-sheh-vich said Serbia no longer recognised the presidency's authority. On the twenty-fifth of March, mee-loh-sheh-vich and tooj-mahn met at ka-ra-jor-jeh-vo. yo-sip ma-no-lich later testified that tooj-mahn had described an agreement in principle concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina. ma-no-lich was not at the meeting. The defence disputed what his account showed about a partition deal. No agreed text has been verified.

Spring 1991. In March 1991, Croatian police and local Serb forces faced each other at pah-krats. The army intervened. No deaths were confirmed. On the thirty-first of March, at the plit-vee-tseh Lakes, Croatian police retook the national park's headquarters. A Croatian policeman, yo-sip yo-vich, and a Serb, rai-ko voo-ka-dee-no-vich, were killed. On the second of May, at bo-ro-vo seh-lo, near voo-ko-var, twelve Croatian policemen were killed. The historical background of the tribunal's merk-shich judgment also reports three Serb civilians killed. On the sixth of May, at a protest in Split, a Yugoslav army soldier, sash-ko geh-shov-skee, was killed.

The twenty-fifth of June. In December 1990, eighty-eight and a half per cent of Slovenia's eligible voters voted for independence. Slovenia's government said it understood independence as carrying out that mandate, after negotiations failed. In May 1991, Croatia voted. Of those who took part, about ninety-three per cent said yes to a sovereign and independent Croatia that could join a union of sovereign republics. Many Serbs boycotted the vote. Krajina's leaders had held their own vote on joining Serbia and remaining in Yugoslavia. Through the spring, the presidents of the six republics met again and again. Slovenia and Croatia wanted a looser union of states. Serbia and Montenegro wanted a federation. Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia proposed a compromise. They found no agreement. In May, Croatia's Stjepan meh-sich was blocked from taking his turn as head of the federal presidency. On the twenty-first of June, the American Secretary of State, James Baker, came to Belgrade and called for unity and democracy. He said: "We worry, frankly, about history repeating itself." On the twenty-fifth of June 1991, the assemblies of Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Two days later, fighting began in Slovenia. That war, and those that followed, are told on the next pages.

Looking back. After tee-toh's death, the federation faced debt, austerity and arguments over money and power. In Serbia, mee-loh-sheh-vich rose on the ko-so-vo question, and Serbia sharply reduced the autonomy of its two provinces. The party that held Yugoslavia together split in 1990. Each republic elected its own leaders. In Croatia, Croatian Serb leaders around k-neen challenged zah-greb's authority and organised a vote on autonomy. Armed incidents began. In June 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Most historians reject the idea that old hatreds made the war inevitable. For decades, Yugoslavs had lived together, worked together and married each other. Susan Woodward stresses debt, austerity and a weakened federal state. V. P. gan-yon stresses leaders who used conflict to hold on to power. Dejan yo-vich stresses how federal authority wore away. These readings overlap. Later, an international tribunal tried some of the people in this story. mee-loh-sheh-vich died in 2006, before his trial ended, so there was no verdict. Milan bah-bich, a Krajina Serb leader, pleaded guilty to persecution. Those trials mostly concerned the wars after June 1991, which are told on the following pages.

Welcome to Battles of History. This is not a battle. It is the background to the battles that follow. In 1980, Yugoslavia was a federation of six republics, with many communities and languages. By the summer of 1991, two of its republics had declared independence. We will show you, slide by slide, how the federation came apart: what was decided, what was said, and what is still argued about. Some chapters describe deaths. We tell them plainly and without detail.

Yugoslavia, 1980 to 1991. On the fourth of May 1980, yo-sip Broz tee-toh died. He had led Yugoslavia since 1945. Eleven years later, on the twenty-fifth of June 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. This page tells what happened in between. The wars that followed are told on the next pages.

Where it is. Yugoslavia lay in south-eastern Europe, on the Adriatic Sea, between Italy and Austria to the north-west and Greece to the south. It belonged to neither the Western alliance nor the Soviet bloc. It had broken with Stalin in 1948, and in 1961 helped found the Non-Aligned Movement.

Six republics, two provinces. Yugoslavia was a federation of six republics: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia. Inside Serbia were two autonomous provinces: voy-vo-dee-na in the north, and ko-so-vo in the south. One party ruled: the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

How this page tells it. Each line is tagged with where it comes from. Some things are in laws and election results. Some are only what one side said. Some were found by a court. We tell you which. Many of these events are remembered very differently by Serbs, Croats, slo-veens, Albanians and others. Where they are, we give each account, and say whose it is.

Many nations. The census of 1981 counted more than twenty-two million people. The largest nations were the Serbs and the Croats. Many others lived alongside them, and some people simply called themselves Yugoslavs. The census used "Muslims" as a category of national identity. bos-nee-ak is the name commonly used today for the community historically associated with that category. The constitution of 1974 gave the republics, and the two provinces, wide powers, and each its own seat on the federal presidency. There was a federal army, the Yugoslav People's Army. Each republic also had its own reserve force, the Territorial Defence.

After tee-toh, tee-toh. tee-toh died in lyoo-blyah-na on the fourth of May 1980. His funeral in Belgrade was attended by many of the world's leaders. After tee-toh died, Yugoslavia's collective presidency became the head of state. It included a representative from every republic and province, and its chair changed every year. "After tee-toh, tee-toh" was the slogan.

Debt. By 1982, Yugoslavia owed foreign lenders more than twenty billion dollars. Austerity followed: shortages, rationed fuel, falling wages, and more people out of work, most of all in the poorer south. Slovenia and Croatia were the richest republics. ko-so-vo was the poorest region. Arguments about who should pay for whom grew sharper.

ko-so-vo, 1981. In March 1981, students at the University of prish-tee-na began to protest. The protests spread. Many demonstrators demanded that ko-so-vo become a republic of its own. A state of emergency was declared. According to official reports cited by the International Commission of Jurists, eight demonstrators and one police officer were killed. Other estimates circulated. ko-so-vo Albanian activists saw the response as repression.

The Memorandum. In the 1980s, ko-so-vo's Albanian majority grew. Many Serbs and Montenegrins left. Serb petitions complained of pressure. Albanians complained of arrests and trials. Why people left varied by place and time, and is still argued about. In September 1986, the Belgrade newspaper veh-cher-nyeh no-vo-stee published excerpts from a leaked draft by members of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts. It argued that Serbs were discriminated against in Yugoslavia, especially in ko-so-vo and Croatia. Serbia's communist leaders at first condemned it. Whether it shaped what came later is a matter of interpretation.

ko-so-vo Polje. On the twenty-fourth of April 1987, at ko-so-vo Polje, Slobodan mee-loh-sheh-vich, the head of Serbia's communist party, met local Serbs who said police had beaten them. He told them: "No one is allowed to beat you." The words were broadcast, and made him famous across Serbia. That September, at a meeting of Serbia's party leaders, mee-loh-sheh-vich's side defeated the group around Serbia's president, Ivan stam-bo-lich, who had been his mentor. stam-bo-lich was removed in December.

The rallies. In 1988 and 1989, huge rallies brought down the leaders of voy-vo-dee-na, and then of Montenegro. Leaders loyal to mee-loh-sheh-vich replaced them. How spontaneous the rallies were is disputed. In February 1989, Albanian miners at trep-cha went on hunger strike against the removal of ko-so-vo's leaders. In March, the assemblies voted for changes to Serbia's constitution that greatly reduced the provinces' self-government. Unrest followed. The official toll was twenty-five dead, including two police officers. Other estimates circulated. ko-so-vo Albanian activists said the vote had been forced. Federal authorities later said their response had answered violence against the police. On the eighth of May 1989, Serbia's assembly elected mee-loh-sheh-vich to chair Serbia's collective presidency.

gah-zee-meh-stahn. On the twenty-eighth of June 1989, six hundred years after the Battle of ko-so-vo, a very large crowd gathered at the gah-zee-meh-stahn monument. mee-loh-sheh-vich said: "Six centuries later, today, we are again fighting battles and facing battles. They are not armed, although even such battles are not yet ruled out." The same speech also spoke of economic, political and cultural prosperity. mee-loh-sheh-vich presented the changes as restoring unity to Serbia. Under the federal constitution, the provinces had exercised broad autonomy.

Slovenia. In 1988, arrests in a case involving a military document sparked protests and the formation of a defence committee. In July, a military court in lyoo-blyah-na tried the journalist Janez yahn-sha and three others. The trial was held in Serbo-Croatian, not in Slovene. In September 1989, Slovenia's assembly declared its right to self-determination. Slovenia banned a rally that the bo-zhoor association of ko-so-vo Serbs had planned in lyoo-blyah-na for the first of December. A boycott of Slovenian goods followed in Serbia.

A new dinar. By 1989, prices were rising so fast that money lost its value from week to week. The OECD put the rise in prices during that year at about two thousand seven hundred per cent. In March 1989, Ante mar-ko-vich became the federal prime minister. On the first of January 1990, mar-ko-vich's government introduced a new dinar, worth ten thousand old ones, and pegged it to the German mark. The World Bank reported that monthly inflation fell close to zero between April and June. But his reforms lost support during 1990.

The last congress. In January 1990, the League of Communists of Yugoslavia met in Belgrade. The Slovenian delegation walked out. The Croatian delegation refused to continue without the slo-veens. A reduced session met again in May, but the party that had ruled Yugoslavia since 1945 never recovered.

In April and May, Slovenia and Croatia voted. In Slovenia, the deh-mos coalition won, and Milan koo-chahn was elected president. In Croatia, Franjo tooj-mahn's Croatian Democratic Union won a clear majority, and the parliament elected him president. In November and December, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Montenegro voted. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, three national parties won most seats. In Serbia, mee-loh-sheh-vich was elected president with about sixty-five per cent. In May 1990, Slovenia's Territorial Defence command ordered weapons moved to federal army depots. Some Slovenian units kept their weapons, and Slovenian authorities secretly organised a defence network. In July, Albanian members of ko-so-vo's assembly, shut out of the building, declared ko-so-vo a republic within Yugoslavia. No federal authority recognised it. Days later, Serbia dissolved ko-so-vo's assembly.
